report:
The evidence on whether ginkgo extract relieves tinnitus symptoms is **mixed and contested**, so a simple "yes" is not well supported by the totality of evidence.

**Cochrane Review (most authoritative):** The 2013 Cochrane systematic review — the gold standard for evidence-based medicine — analyzed four trials with 1,543 participants and concluded there was **no reliable evidence** that ginkgo biloba reduces tinnitus severity compared to placebo. ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus))

**Systematic review supporting EGb 761:** A separate systematic review of randomized, placebo-controlled trials found evidence of efficacy specifically for the standardized extract **EGb 761®**, based on three trials in patients with tinnitus. However, it noted that efficacy of other ginkgo preparations has not been proven. ([NCBI/PubMed](https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK98818/))

**Negative trial:** A double-blind placebo-controlled study found that ginkgo extract LI 1370 had **no greater therapeutic effect than placebo** for tinnitus. ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC26593/))

**Recent open-label study (2025):** An uncontrolled, open-label study of 170 patients taking EGb 761® for 24 weeks suggested some benefit, but the lack of a placebo control limits conclusions. ([MDPI/JCM](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/1/87))

**Bottom line:** The most rigorous evidence (Cochrane) does not support ginkgo as an effective tinnitus treatment. Some trials of the specific standardized extract EGb 761® show modest positive results, but these are offset by negative findings and methodological limitations. The answer is closer to **"possibly, for a specific extract, but overall evidence is weak and inconclusive"** than a clear "yes."
